The absorber is based on a Salisbury screen topology but replaces the resistive sheet with an active frequency selective surface (FSS) controlled by PIN diodes.
The FSS consists of 180 dipole elements arranged on a rectangular lattice on a 0.8 mm thick printed circuit board.
PIN diodes used are Phillips BA585 surface-mount devices acting as current-controlled resistors at microwave frequencies.
The dielectric spacer is 4.0 mm thick Rhocell 51 foam with relative permittivity ε_r = 1.05 and loss tangent tanδ = 0.0017.
The total thickness of the absorber is less than 5.0 mm.
Reflectivity can be tuned from strongly reflecting to less than -20 dB over 9.5 to 12.5 GHz by adjusting the diode bias current.
Bias currents required for tuning are very low, typically below 1 mA, resulting in power consumption less than 25 µW/cm².
The absorber shows a double null reflectivity response with increasing bias current before saturating back to a reflecting state.
The transmission line model uses a series RLC circuit to represent the FSS impedance with fixed inductance and capacitance and variable resistance.
Typical inductance and capacitance values used in modeling are around 3.4–4.7 nH and 4.9–9.1 fF respectively.
The absorber can be switched at rates exceeding 20 MHz due to the fast response of the PIN diodes (time constants ~10 ns).
The active FSS provides a reactive impedance component that allows a thinner absorber with increased bandwidth compared to a purely resistive Salisbury screen.
The sheet impedance tuning is achieved electrically, avoiding mechanical adjustments of spacer thickness or permittivity.
Experimental measurements were performed in a calibrated NRL arch using an HP 8510C network analyzer.
The design reduces diode density and power consumption by using a single active FSS layer instead of multiple PIN diode layers.
The absorber is designed for single linear polarization operation.
The reflectivity null occurs when the sheet impedance equals the free space impedance and the dielectric spacer thickness is λ/4 at the design frequency.
The structure includes an outer dielectric skin formed by the circuit board, which also protects the diodes.
The active absorber can be used for adaptive radar cross section (RCS) control in military and civilian applications.
The authors reference prior work on active absorbers and frequency selective surfaces for context and design methodology.
